lessons.title: What a financial model is
lessons.summary: Inputs, calculations and outputs: the anatomy of every model.

steps.title: A model is a structured calculator
steps.body:
A financial model is a set of linked calculations that turns assumptions (inputs you can change, such as the room rate) into results (outputs you decide with, such as revenue).

Every good model has three parts: inputs (what we assume), calculations (how one thing leads to another) and outputs (what we report). Because the parts are linked, changing one input updates every result that depends on it.
steps.deeper: Professionals build models to answer decision questions: Should we raise prices? Can we afford this loan? What happens if demand falls 10%? A model does not predict the future. It shows the consequences of assumptions, so the quality of the answer depends on the quality of the assumptions and the logic. That is why models separate inputs from calculations: anyone can see what was assumed and challenge it.

steps.title: A tiny hotel model
steps.body: The fictional Harbour Crest Hotel sold 70 rooms last night at an average rate of $200. Revenue is a calculation, not an input: it comes from the two assumptions.
steps.note: If the rate changes to $210, B3 updates to $14,700 with no retyping.

steps.title: Your turn: link the revenue
steps.prompt: In B3, write a formula for room revenue using the inputs in B1 and B2.
hints: Revenue = quantity x price.
Multiply the cell holding rooms sold by the cell holding the rate.
Type =B1*B2
steps.solution: =B1*B2 multiplies rooms sold by the rate. Because it uses cell references, it updates when either input changes.

steps.question: If the average rate rises by 10% and rooms sold stay the same, what happens to room revenue?
steps.reveal: Revenue = rooms x rate. With rooms fixed, revenue changes in exact proportion to the rate.

steps.title: Move the drivers
steps.prompt: Change the rate and the rooms sold. Watch revenue respond.
steps.observe: Set the rate to 220 (10% above 200): revenue moves from $14,000 to $15,400, exactly 10% higher.

steps.title: Why linking matters
steps.body: Your prediction is tested by the model itself: with rooms fixed, a 10% rate increase gives exactly 10% more revenue. This only works because B3 calculates from B1 and B2.
steps.misconception: A common mistake is typing 14000 into the revenue cell. It looks right today, but the next time an assumption changes the model silently shows a wrong number. FinPilot checks your formulas with changed inputs to catch this.

steps.title: The manager's question
steps.scenario: The general manager wants to know tonight's revenue if the hotel sells 64 rooms at $220.
steps.question: What is the room revenue in dollars?

mistakes.message: You added rooms and rate. Revenue is rooms multiplied by rate.

hints: Revenue = rooms sold x average rate.

questions.question: Which of these is an input (assumption) in a hotel revenue model?
options: Average daily rate assumed for next month
explanations: Room revenue is calculated from rooms sold and rate.
Total revenue is the sum of calculated revenue lines.
A variance is calculated by comparing two results.
questions.explanation: Inputs are the values you assume; everything else should be calculated from them.

questions.question: Why do professional models keep inputs separate from calculations?
options: To make the workbook look tidy only
So assumptions are visible, easy to change and easy to challenge
questions.explanation: Separating inputs lets reviewers see and test every assumption, and prevents hidden hard-coded numbers.

points: A model turns assumptions into results through linked calculations.
Inputs, calculations and outputs should be clearly separated.
Formulas must reference input cells, never retype their values.
formulas: Room revenue = Rooms sold x Average rate

lessons.title: The three financial statements
lessons.summary: Income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, and how they connect.

steps.title: Three views of one business
steps.body:
Income statement: performance over a period (revenue minus expenses = profit).
Balance sheet: position at a point in time. What the business owns (assets) equals what it owes (liabilities) plus what belongs to the owners (equity).
Cash flow statement: how cash moved during the period, split into operating, investing and financing activities.
steps.deeper: The statements are linked. Net income from the income statement increases retained earnings, which is part of equity on the balance sheet. The closing cash on the cash flow statement must equal the cash line on the balance sheet. If a model's balance sheet does not balance, a link is broken somewhere; a professional never 'plugs' the gap with an unexplained number.

steps.title: Harbour Crest's balance sheet (fictional, $)
steps.body: The accounting equation always holds: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
steps.note: Equity is the residual: what would be left for owners if all assets were sold at book value and all debts paid.

steps.title: Calculate equity
steps.prompt: In B3, calculate equity from total assets (B1) and total liabilities (B2).
hints: Rearrange Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
Equity = Assets - Liabilities.
Type =B1-B2
steps.solution: =B1-B2. Equity is what remains after liabilities are deducted from assets.

steps.question: The hotel borrows an extra $1,000,000 from the bank and keeps it as cash. What happens to equity?
steps.reveal: Assets (cash) and liabilities (loan) both rise by $1,000,000, so equity is unchanged. Borrowing is not income.

steps.title: Borrow and see
steps.prompt: Increase the bank loan and the cash together, then try changing only other assets.
steps.observe: Raise cash and liabilities by the same amount: equity stays at $1,800,000, but debt-to-equity rises, so the hotel is riskier.

steps.title: Financing is not profit
steps.body: Borrowing changes the mix of how assets are funded, not the owners' stake. Equity changes through profit (or loss), owner investment and dividends.
steps.misconception: Cash in the bank is not profit. A hotel can hold plenty of borrowed cash while losing money, or be profitable with almost no cash.

steps.title: Roll forward retained earnings
steps.scenario: Harbour Crest opened the year with retained earnings of $1,200,000. It earned net income of $250,000 and paid dividends of $100,000.
steps.question: What are closing retained earnings?

mistakes.message: You did not deduct the dividends. Dividends paid to owners reduce retained earnings.
You added the dividends. Dividends are a distribution to owners, so they reduce retained earnings.

hints: Closing = Opening + Net income - Dividends.

questions.question: Which statement shows the financial position at a single point in time?
questions.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot; the income statement and cash flow cover a period.

questions.question: Where does net income go on the balance sheet?
questions.explanation: Net income increases retained earnings. Cash changes separately, through the cash flow statement.

points: Income statement = performance over a period.
Balance sheet = position at a point in time; Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
Cash flow statement explains the change in cash.
Net income links to retained earnings; closing cash links to the balance sheet.
formulas: Closing retained earnings = Opening + Net income - Dividends

lessons.title: Profit versus cash flow
lessons.summary: Why a profitable hotel can run short of cash.

steps.title: Earned is not the same as received
steps.body:
Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash has moved. Cash accounting records only cash in and out.

Profit follows accrual rules. Cash follows the bank account. The gap comes from timing (customers paying later), non-cash expenses (depreciation) and spending that is not an expense yet (buying equipment, repaying loans).
steps.deeper: Operating cash flow (indirect method) starts from net income and adjusts: add back depreciation (an expense with no cash payment), subtract increases in receivables and inventory (cash tied up), add increases in payables (bills not yet paid). Investing (capex) and financing (loans, dividends) then explain the rest of the cash movement.

steps.title: A profitable month with falling cash ($)
steps.body: Harbour Crest hosted several corporate events billed on 60-day terms and bought new fitness equipment.

rows: Corporate clients have not paid yet

steps.note: Profit of $120,000, but $120,000 less cash in the bank.

steps.title: Build operating cash flow
steps.prompt: In B6, calculate operating cash flow from the five items above it (B1:B5 hold positive amounts; think about which direction each one moves cash).
hints: Start with net income and add back the non-cash expense.
Increases in receivables and inventory use cash (subtract). An increase in payables keeps cash in the business (add).
Type =B1+B2-B3-B4+B5

steps.question: Corporate clients start paying in 90 days instead of 30. Revenue and profit are unchanged. What happens to this month's operating cash flow?
options: No change, because profit is unchanged
steps.reveal: Slower payment raises receivables. A larger increase in receivables reduces operating cash flow even though profit is the same.

steps.title: Stretch the payment terms
steps.prompt: Increase the receivables build-up and watch operating cash flow, while net income stays fixed.
steps.observe: Push receivables to $300,000: operating cash flow turns negative while profit still shows $120,000.

steps.title: Timing, non-cash items and investment
steps.body: Profit measures whether the business earns more than it costs. Cash measures whether it can pay its bills. Both matter: a hotel can be profitable and still miss payroll if customers pay late or if it spends heavily on renovation.
steps.misconception: Depreciation is added back not because it 'creates' cash, but because it reduced profit without any cash leaving. The cash left earlier, when the asset was bought (capex).

steps.title: Check a month's cash
steps.scenario: Another month: net income $80,000, depreciation $30,000, receivables increased by $140,000, payables increased by $10,000, inventory unchanged.
steps.question: What is operating cash flow? (Use a minus sign for an outflow.)

mistakes.message: You added the increase in receivables. Money owed by customers is not yet cash; an increase uses cash, so subtract it.
You subtracted depreciation. Depreciation reduced profit without a cash payment, so it is added back.
You subtracted the increase in payables. Bills not yet paid keep cash in the business, so add it.

hints: OCF = Net income + Depreciation - Increase in receivables + Increase in payables.

questions.question: Which item can make cash flow lower than profit?
questions.explanation: Rising receivables means revenue was recorded but not yet collected.

questions.question: Under accrual accounting, when is a hotel room night recorded as revenue?
options: When the guest stays (the service is delivered)
When the credit card payment settles
At the end of the year
questions.explanation: Revenue is recognised when it is earned, which for a room is the night of the stay. A deposit received earlier is a liability until then.

points: Accrual profit and cash flow differ because of timing, non-cash items and investment.
Increases in receivables and inventory use cash; increases in payables provide cash.
Depreciation is added back in the indirect method.
Capex and loan repayments reduce cash but are not expenses in the period.
formulas: OCF = Net income + D&A - ΔReceivables - ΔInventory + ΔPayables
Change in cash = OCF - Capex + Net financing

lessons.title: Cost behaviour and break-even
lessons.summary: Fixed and variable costs, contribution margin and break-even occupancy.

steps.title: Costs that move and costs that stay
steps.body:
Variable costs rise with volume: housekeeping supplies, laundry, amenities and booking commissions for each occupied room. Fixed costs stay the same within a normal range of activity: management salaries, insurance, property tax, base maintenance.

Contribution margin = price - variable cost per unit. It is what each extra room night contributes towards fixed costs and then profit. Break-even volume = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit.
steps.deeper: Real costs are often semi-variable (part fixed, part variable) and 'fixed' only within a relevant range: a hotel that runs at 95% may need extra staff. Break-even assumes a constant price and mix, so treat it as a guide, not a precise threshold. If price is at or below variable cost, contribution is zero or negative and break-even does not exist.

steps.title: Harbour Crest monthly break-even
steps.body: Average room rate $250; variable cost per occupied room $45; fixed monthly costs $600,000.
steps.note: Below 2,927 room nights in the month the hotel loses money on this simplified view.

steps.title: Break-even room nights
steps.prompt: In B4, calculate break-even room nights from the price (B1), variable cost per room (B2) and fixed costs (B3).
hints: Break-even = fixed costs / contribution per unit.
Contribution per unit = price - variable cost. Use brackets so the subtraction happens first.
Type =B3/(B1-B2)
steps.solution: =B3/(B1-B2) = 2,926.83 room nights. Without brackets, =B3/B1-B2 divides first and gives a meaningless result.

steps.question: Laundry and amenity costs rise, increasing the variable cost per room. What happens to break-even room nights?
options: Unchanged, because fixed costs did not change
steps.reveal: Higher variable cost shrinks the contribution per room, so more rooms are needed to cover the same fixed costs.

steps.title: Find the break-even
steps.prompt: Change price, variable cost and fixed costs.
steps.observe: Set variable cost equal to price: break-even shows #N/A because each room contributes nothing, so no volume can cover fixed costs.

steps.title: Operating leverage
steps.body: Hotels have high fixed costs, so once break-even is passed, most of each extra room's revenue becomes profit. The same leverage works in reverse: a small drop in occupancy can wipe out profit quickly.
steps.misconception: Break-even is not the target. It is the floor. Managers also consider cash commitments (loan repayments) that break-even on profit ignores.

steps.title: Break-even occupancy
steps.scenario: A 150-room hotel has 4,500 available room nights in a 30-day month. Fixed costs are $520,000, the average rate is $230 and variable cost is $38 per occupied room.
steps.question: What occupancy does it need to break even? (Enter as a percentage, e.g. 61.5%.)

mistakes.message: You divided fixed costs by the full rate. Each room only contributes rate minus variable cost ($192).
That is the break-even number of room nights. Divide it by the 4,500 available room nights to get occupancy.

hints: First find break-even room nights: fixed / (rate - variable cost).
Then divide by available room nights.

questions.question: Which hotel cost is most likely variable?
questions.explanation: Amenities are consumed for each occupied room, so they move with volume.

questions.question: Price $180, variable cost $30, fixed costs $300,000. Break-even units?

mistakes.message: You divided by the price. Use the contribution per unit: $180 - $30 = $150.

points: Variable costs move with volume; fixed costs do not (within a relevant range).
Contribution margin = price - variable cost.
Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit; undefined if contribution is zero or negative.
formulas: Contribution per unit = Price - Variable cost
Break-even units = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit
Break-even revenue = Fixed costs / CM ratio

lessons.title: Margins, EBITDA, EBIT and net income
lessons.summary: Different profit measures answer different questions.

steps.title: A ladder of profit measures
steps.body:
Gross profit = revenue - cost of sales (the direct cost of what was sold). Gross margin = gross profit / revenue.
EBITDA = earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation: revenue minus all operating expenses except D&A.
EBIT = EBITDA - depreciation and amortisation.
Net income = EBIT - interest - tax.
steps.deeper: These measures are not interchangeable. In a hotel, room revenue is one revenue stream; total operating revenue adds F&B and other departments; departmental profit deducts each department's direct costs; EBITDA also deducts undistributed costs such as administration, sales and maintenance; net income deducts depreciation, interest and tax; and cash flow adjusts for timing and investment. EBITDA is popular for comparing operating performance because it ignores financing and accounting choices, but it is not cash: it ignores capex, working capital, interest and tax.

steps.title: Harbour Crest income statement (fictional, $)
steps.body: One quarter of results.
steps.note: Each step down the ladder deducts a different kind of cost.

steps.title: EBITDA margin
steps.prompt: In B4, calculate the EBITDA margin: EBITDA as a share of revenue. Revenue is in B1, cost of sales in B2 and other operating expenses (excluding D&A) in B3.
hints: EBITDA = revenue - cost of sales - other operating expenses.
Margin = EBITDA / revenue. Bracket the subtraction.
Type =(B1-B2-B3)/B1

steps.question: The hotel refinances its loan at a higher interest rate. Which measures change?
options: Only net income (and profit before tax)
steps.reveal: Interest sits below EBIT, so EBITDA and EBIT are unaffected. Net income falls (partly offset by lower tax).

steps.title: Walk down the ladder
steps.prompt: Change costs and financing and see which lines move.
steps.observe: Double interest to $200,000: EBITDA and EBIT stay at $700,000 and $500,000; net income falls from $300,000 to $225,000.

steps.title: Choose the measure for the question
steps.body: Comparing two hotels' operating performance? EBITDA margin. Judging the owners' return? Net income. Paying the bills? Cash flow. Pricing a menu? Gross margin.
steps.misconception: 'EBITDA is cash' is a common error. A hotel with strong EBITDA can still run out of cash if it must replace roofs and furniture (capex) or repay debt.

steps.title: Restaurant gross margin
steps.scenario: The hotel restaurant had revenue of $1,800,000 and cost of food and beverage sold of $630,000.
steps.question: What is the restaurant's gross margin?

mistakes.message: 35% is the cost of sales ratio. Gross margin is what is left after cost of sales: 1 - 35% = 65%.
$1,170,000 is gross profit in dollars. Divide it by revenue to get the margin.

hints: Gross margin = (revenue - cost of sales) / revenue.

questions.question: Which measure deducts depreciation but not interest or tax?
questions.explanation: EBIT = earnings before interest and tax; depreciation has already been deducted.

questions.question: Room revenue at Harbour Crest is $1.6m in May. Which statement is true?
options: Room revenue is one revenue stream; total revenue also includes F&B and other departments
questions.explanation: Revenue lines, profit measures and cash are different things and must not be used interchangeably.

points: Gross profit, EBITDA, EBIT and net income each deduct a further layer of cost.
EBITDA is an operating measure, not cash.
Room revenue, total revenue, departmental profit, EBITDA, net income and cash flow are distinct.
formulas: Gross margin = (Revenue - Cost of sales) / Revenue

lessons.title: Growth rates and ratios
lessons.summary: Percent change, percentage points and compounding.

steps.title: Measuring change
steps.body:
Growth rate = (current - prior) / prior. It shows change relative to the starting point.

When the measure is already a percentage (like occupancy), say whether you mean percentage points (70% to 77% is +7 points) or percent change (+7 / 70 = +10%).
steps.deeper: Growth rates compound: two years of 10% growth is 21%, not 20%. The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) = (end / start)^(1/years) - 1. Growth from a negative or zero base is not meaningful; report it as n/a and describe the change in amounts instead.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body: Fictional Harbour Crest figures.
steps.note: Always say which kind of change you are reporting.

steps.title: Growth rate formula
steps.prompt: In B3, calculate the growth rate from last year's revenue (B1) to this year's (B2).
hints: Change divided by the starting value.
Bracket the subtraction: (new - old) / old.
Type =(B2-B1)/B1

steps.question: Revenue falls 20% one year and rises 20% the next. Where does it end up?
steps.reveal: 100 x 0.8 = 80, then 80 x 1.2 = 96: 4% below. The rise is measured from a smaller base.

steps.title: Compounding
steps.prompt: Try different pairs of growth rates.
steps.observe: Try +10% and +10%: total change is 21%, not 20%.

steps.title: Base effects
steps.body: Every percentage needs a base. Decreases and increases of the same percentage do not cancel because they apply to different bases.
steps.misconception: Saying 'occupancy grew 7%' when it moved from 70% to 77% confuses readers. That is 7 percentage points, or 10%.

steps.title: Report occupancy growth
steps.question: What is the percent change in occupancy (not percentage points)?

mistakes.message: 8 is the change in percentage points. The question asks for the percent change: 8 / 64 = 12.5%.
You divided by the new value. Growth is measured against the starting value (64%).

hints: (new - old) / old.

questions.question: Revenue grows from $4.0m to $4.84m over two years. What is the CAGR?

mistakes.message: 21% is the total growth over two years. CAGR is the steady annual rate: (4.84/4)^(1/2) - 1 = 10%.
You halved the total growth. Growth compounds, so take the square root of the growth factor instead.

questions.question: Last year's EBITDA was -$50,000 and this year it is $100,000. How should you report growth?
options: Growth is not meaningful from a negative base; report the $150,000 improvement
questions.explanation: Percent change from a negative or zero base is misleading. Report the amounts.

points: Growth = (current - prior) / prior.
Distinguish percentage points from percent change.
Growth compounds; use CAGR for multi-year rates.
Do not compute growth from zero or negative bases.

lessons.title: Project: Profitable but short of cash
lessons.summary: Explain to the owner why Harbour Crest reported a profit but ran short of cash.

steps.title: Business context
steps.body: The owner of the fictional Harbour Crest Hotel is puzzled. The September income statement shows a healthy profit, yet the bank balance fell sharply and the hotel had to use its overdraft to pay suppliers. Your task: quantify why, and write a short explanation with a recommendation.
steps.deeper: Objectives: (1) rebuild operating cash flow from the data, (2) calculate the change in cash, (3) identify the primary cause, (4) recommend actions. All figures are fictional.

steps.title: September data ($, fictional)
steps.body: Extracted from the management accounts.
steps.note: Receivables jumped after a large conference was invoiced on 60-day terms.

questions.question: By how much did accounts receivable increase?
What is operating cash flow for September? (OCF = NI + D&A - ΔAR - ΔInventory + ΔAP)

mistakes.message: Payables fell by $35,000, which uses cash. A decrease in payables is subtracted (ΔAP is negative).
Check the inventory movement: it increased by $15,000, which uses cash.

questions.question: What is the total change in cash for the month (operating cash flow, capex and loan repayment)?
What is closing cash? (A negative number means an overdraft.)
What is the single largest reason cash fell while profit was positive?
options: The $310,000 increase in receivables from the conference invoice
questions.explanation: The receivables build-up ($310,000) alone exceeds net income. Capex ($180,000) is the second-largest factor.

steps.title: Task 3: explain it to the owner
steps.prompt: Write 4-6 sentences for the owner: explain why profit and cash differ this month, quantify the main drivers and recommend at least two actions.

rubric.criterion: Quantifies with at least two numbers

steps.model_answer: September profit was $210,000, but cash fell by $325,000 to an overdraft of $175,000. Profit records the conference revenue when it was earned, while the client will pay in 60 days: receivables rose by $310,000, more than the month's profit. The $180,000 room refurbishment and the $60,000 loan repayment used further cash but are not expenses this month. Paying suppliers faster (payables down $35,000) also used cash. I recommend requiring deposits for large events, shortening corporate payment terms or chasing the conference invoice, and phasing future refurbishment spend to match collections. A 13-week cash forecast would warn of shortfalls before they happen.

points: Working capital timing can outweigh profit in a single month.
Capex and debt repayments use cash without hitting profit.
Quantify each driver and connect it to an action.
formulas: Change in cash = OCF - Capex - Debt repayment
